extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and philosophers working in philosophy of mathematics and related areas (philosophy of science, metaphysics, epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic framework for evaluating forms of naturalism (methodological, ontological, epistemological) as applied to mathematics; explains variants, motivations, problems, and how standards from science and mathematics should be applied or balanced in philosophy of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three main naturalisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary philosophy’s three main naturalisms are methodological, ontological and epistemological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological naturalism concerns which standards (e.g., science or mathematics) are authoritative; ontological naturalism concerns whether all entities are in some sense natural (e.g., spatiotemporal); epistemological naturalism concerns whether valid methods of inquiry are natural. The entry concentrates on methodological naturalism and treats the other two more briefly (see section 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses of methodological naturalism (scientific/mathematical/mathematical-cum-scientific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological naturalism has three principal senses: (1) the only authoritative standards are those of natural science (scientific naturalism); (2) the only authoritative standards are those of mathematics itself (mathematical naturalism); (3) an amalgam in which the authoritative standards are those of both natural science and mathematics (mathematical-cum-scientific naturalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the entry ‘science’ refers to the natural sciences. These three readings shape how claims in mathematics and the philosophy of mathematics are to be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Anti-Revisionism
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalism tends to have anti-revisionary consequences for mathematics: approaches that recommend radical revisions to mathematical methodology, ontology, epistemology or accepted theorems (e.g., intuitionism) are ruled out if not sanctioned by scientific or mathematical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Brouwerian intuitionism and Dummettian arguments are rejected by naturalists because scientific and mathematical practice arguably sanction classical mathematics; naturalists block 'fanciful attacks' on disciplines by less secure methodologies. Nevertheless, naturalists accept some theory revision that occurs within mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative claim readings: Biconditional Naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Biconditional Naturalism: accept p iff p is sanctioned by X-standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the strongest reading: valid standards just are X-standards. If X-standards are taken as definitive, no other standards matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative claim readings: Trumping Naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Trumping Naturalism: accept p if p is sanctioned by X-standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows that a statement may be acceptable even if X-standards do not sanction it; in practice, often glossed as 'when science (or mathematics) speaks with a firm and unified voice, the philosopher is obliged to accept its conclusions or offer recognizably scientific reasons for resisting them' (Burgess & Rosen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative claim readings: Emphasis Naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis Naturalism: in assessing whether p, give more emphasis to X-standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vague doctrine with degrees; modest versions capture naturalistically-inclined philosophers who do not fully endorse stronger readings. Biconditional naturalism is recovered when X-standards are emphasised so strongly that no others matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative claim readings: Compatibility Naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Compatibility Naturalism: do not accept p if p is incompatible with X-standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaker than trumping: if p is sanctioned by X-standards then compatibility naturalism enjoins non-acceptance of ¬p but does not necessarily enjoin acceptance of p (suspension of judgment remains an option). This view is generally accepted by most contemporary philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary problem (X-standards vs non-X-standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalism sets up an opposition between X-standards (scientific, mathematical, or scientific-cum-mathematical) and other types of standards; but there are no sharp boundaries between science and non-science or between mathematics and non-mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transitions from physics to philosophy of physics to metaphysics; different kinds of mathematical writing (research articles, textbooks, popular books) blur the line. Naturalists may try to argue for a sufficiently sharp but hard-to-define boundary, or treat distinctions piecemeal (cf. Maddy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological unity / fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether there are global scientific standards or only domain-specific standards (e.g., physics-naturalism, biology-naturalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If standards fragment, scientific naturalism may fracture into competing naturalisms. A rigorous naturalist should show either why a single set of standards is appropriate or provide case studies to shore up the assumption of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of sanction (gradualism of standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific (and perhaps mathematical) standards sanction propositions to degrees rather than absolutely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simple black-or-white notion of 'sanctioned / not sanctioned' is inadequate. Naturalists must issue guidelines for apportioning credence in p in line with the degree and type of commitment that scientific or mathematical standards recommend (Bayesian confirmation theory is relevant). Examples: Goldbach's Conjecture may be highly supported non-deductively yet not proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards vs practitioners (what X-practitioners believe vs what X-standards sanction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate what X-standards sanction with what X-practitioners in fact believe; practitioners may not have considered a question or may be wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tighter connection: what X-standards sanction is what X-practitioners are disposed to correctly believe qua X-practitioners. In practice, practitioners' beliefs are good defeasible evidence for standards, but special pleading would be required to attribute widespread error to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader naturalisms and balancing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Broader naturalisms extend the naturalist umbrella to social sciences, semantics, psychology, linguistics, etc.; this introduces multiple potentially competing standards that must be balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad naturalist might weight natural sciences vs semantics (example: 2/3 vs 1/3) or require unanimity across sciences. Mathematical-cum-scientific naturalists especially need policies for weighing mathematical and scientific pros and cons (e.g., the clash between ontological economy and Maddy’s MAXIMIZE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster of scientific principles as candidate standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific standards often invoked include empirical adequacy, ontological economy (parsimony), simplicity, fertility, and related virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles come in different versions and balancing them is non-trivial. Debates include whether scientific appeals to ontological parsimony extend to abstract objects, and how to balance competing desiderata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation by success (marks of disciplinary success)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discipline's success might be a motivation for naturalism: (i) a widely shared conception among practitioners of guiding questions and methodology; (ii) progress within the discipline in addressing its guiding questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But measuring success in this way risks question-begging or relativism: many internally coherent but epistemically unacceptable 'disciplines' could register as successful on these metrics unless 'success' is more carefully specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation by agreement / tractability
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalists may argue that science/mathematics usually reach broad agreement (or have tractable disagreement), so their standards are preferable to philosophical ones that lead to persistent disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This appeal is contested: agreement can be produced by non-epistemic forces; more plausible arguments should focus on the explanation of why agreement obtains or on tractability in idealised epistemic subjects, but these may beg the question or be controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary vs conservative consequences of naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalism is conservative in some respects (blocks external revision of mathematics) but revolutionary in others (advocating replacement of standards used to judge mathematics or its philosophy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific naturalism about mathematics proper is philosophically revolutionary because it advocates scientific standards where mathematical standards are traditional; mathematical naturalism is philosophically revolutionary (if mathematicians are platonists it closes further philosophical debate) while mathematically conservative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing mathematical and scientific standards (practical policy requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical-cum-scientific naturalists must provide a general policy for dealing with potential clashes between mathematical and scientific standards (e.g., ontological economy vs MAXIMIZE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosophy of mathematics lacks an established tradition for weighing such pros and cons; the naturalist must either propose balancing rules or argue clashes cannot arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological naturalism: natural science as arbiter of ontology / spatiotemporal constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Ontological naturalism holds that natural science is the arbiter of ontology and (in stronger versions) that all entities are spatiotemporal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reductionist versions attempt to identify mathematical objects with spatiotemporal entities; such views face problems like the cardinality problem and clash with mathematical method, making ontological naturalism unpopular in these forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems for reductionist ontological naturalism (cardinality, contingency, aggregates of aggregates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductionist accounts (e.g., Millian accounts) face difficulties: (i) cardinality problem—identifying numbers with concrete aggregates yields wrong cardinalities; (ii) contingency problem—mathematical truths become contingent on spatiotemporal facts; (iii) dilemmas about aggregates of aggregates (higher-order aggregates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses include modalising the account (Kitcher) or theoretical identifications, but these are significant objections that make reductionist ontological naturalism problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalist Anti-Platonism and epistemological challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Ontological naturalists often deny platonism; the main argument is epistemological: if mathematical objects are abstract and causally inert, it's unclear how we can know them (Benacerraf-style problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalist-platonists respond by (a) denying the existence of a simple criterion for knowledge that rules out abstract-object knowledge, and (b) adopting a Quinean holistic line that treats belief in abstract mathematical entities as part of our best scientific theory and so arrived at by a reliable method (scientific method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-deductive grounds and credence in mathematical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical belief is not always deductive; non-deductive grounds (e.g., empirical support, explanatory considerations) can justify graded credence in mathematical claims (e.g., Goldbach’s Conjecture is supported to a high degree absent a proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalists must articulate how to apportion credence according to the type and degree of commitment recommended by scientific or mathematical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecemeal or stance-based naturalism (Maddy's Second Philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalism can be framed as a stance or piecemeal method of inquiry rather than a blanket doctrine—accepting standards piecemeal depending on the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stance-based approach treats naturalism as a methodological orientation that seeks to build on accepted disciplinary practices rather than imposing an overarching philosophical rule; it may avoid some boundary problems but raises challenges about justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mathematics proper and philosophy of mathematics as evaluation domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Different claims should be assessed by different standards: statements in mathematics proper (e.g., proofs like the Green–Tao theorem) are assessed by mathematical standards, while philosophical claims about existence or permissibility (e.g., platonism, impredicativity) are assessed by philosophical standards which naturalists argue should be scientific or mathematical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quine's approach treats mathematical results as acceptable if they are part of the best systematisation of science; the entry stresses the need to distinguish evaluation domains and the standards appropriate to each.
